problem.paragraph: If $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}f(x)$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}f(x)$$ both exist, then $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}f(x)$$ exists.
If $$f(5)$$ is not defined, then $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5^{-}}f(x)$$ does not exist.
Suppose the function $$f$$ is defined on the interval $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ . If $$f(a)$$ and $$f(b)$$ have the same sign, then $$f$$ has no zero in $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ .
If $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x) = L$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x) = L$$ , then $$f(a) = L$$ .
If $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$ and $$g(a) = M$$ , then $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)g(x) = \mathit{LM}$$ .
If $$f$$ is continuous for all $$x \neq 0$$ and $$f(0) = 0$$ , then $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}f(x) = 0$$ .
If $$f$$ and $$g$$ are both discontinuous at $$a$$ , then $$f + g$$ must be discontinuous at $$a$$ .
If $$f$$ and $$g$$ are both discontinuous at $$a$$ , then $$\mathit{fg}$$ must be discontinuous at $$a$$ .
If $$g \circ f$$ is continuous at $$a$$ , then $$f$$ must be continuous at $$a$$ and $$g$$ must be continuous at $$f(a)$$ .
If $$f$$ is discontinuous at $$a$$ and $$g$$ is discontinuous at $$f(a)$$ , then $$g \circ f$$ must be discontinuous at $$a$$ .

Is the following statement true or false? Suppose $$f$$ is continuous on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ and $$f(a) < f(b)$$ . If $$M$$ is a number that lies outside the interval $$\left\lbrack f(a),f(b) \right\rbrack$$ , then there does not exist a number $$a < c < b$$ such that $$f(c) = M$$ . Does this contradict the Intermediate Value Theorem?
